claims.text: Potential pulsing induces reversible dynamic surface oxidation in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts.
Dynamic surface oxidation modulates the d-band center of key active sites.
Potential-pulse-induced oxidation improves ethanol oxidation performance by facilitating removal of carbonaceous poisoning species.
Potential-pulse-induced oxidation alters ethanol oxidation product selectivity.
Under constant-potential operation, the catalyst has a stable surface oxidation-state distribution.
The controlled change is cycling between the ethanol-oxidation potential and 1.2 V versus RHE for 30-second pulses.
The proposed test is conducted in 0.5 M H2SO4 at ambient temperature.
High-potential pulses transiently and preferentially oxidize Rh and Ru surface sites.
Potential pulsing reversibly changes local surface coordination through surface reconstruction.
Transient oxidation shifts the d-band center of the affected sites.
A pulse-induced d-band-center shift changes the binding affinities of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Changes in catalyst surface composition or state can affect catalytic performance.
The altered binding affinities facilitate removal of carbonaceous poisoning species.
The altered surface favors acetic acid over less-completely oxidized products.
Relative to constant-potential operation, pulsing will produce in situ XAS signatures of transient oxidation and reduction.
Relative to constant-potential operation, pulsing will enhance tolerance to carbonaceous poisoning.
Relative to constant-potential operation, pulsing will increase the acetic-acid yield.
The mechanism should hold at ambient temperature in 0.5 M H2SO4 when pulse parameters cause reversible oxidation rather than irreversible degradation.
The magnitude of the d-band-center shift and the boundary between reversible oxidation and irreversible degradation are uncertain.

The hypothesis is falsified if pulsing produces neither significant transient oxidation-state changes nor statistically distinguishable changes in activity, poisoning tolerance, or selectivity relative to the constant-potential control.
